Q: Why usually the return address's value is stored in the stack pointer with offset 12 ? Why can't we simply store it in the fist 4 bytes of the stack? A:

add sp, sp, -16 reserves 16 bytes. Storing to 12(sp) after that puts the return address at the very top of your stack frame, which seems like a good place for it. All your local vars can go below that, along with any outgoing stack args to callees where the args don't all fit in registers.
(If this is a leaf function, you don't need to save/restore the return address, it can just stay in the link register like in your fun2)

In a variadic function with some stack args, it might make sense to put the return address elsewhere so you can dump the register args contiguous with the stack args.

(I don't know if there are any RISC-V calling-convention requirements on stack-frame layout that constrains where you should save the return address. Perhaps if you're also using a frame pointer, there's a standard layout that would form a linked-list, like there is on x86 where call pushes the return address itself, and the usual convention is to save the caller's frame-pointer register right below that if using one.)

Q: How to change package library location on arduino ide A:

In old Arduino IDE 1.?.x you could just download it as zip file, unpack, create directory called portable inside and sketches, libraries and platforms were installed into this directory. But it might be not supported anymore by esp core.

This doesn't work in 2.x (at least it wasn't when I was checking it about a year ago).

The arduino-cli seems to have possibilities to specify locations as platforms (cores) by environment variables or maybe even some configuration file (esp32 "library" is whole infrastructure for it)

There might be some workarounds, for example:

  • symlinks on linux

  • windows has some too, but I'm not sure if you can symlink different drive and if it needs to be ntfs

  • you might be able to start arduino with changed environment variable with user profile location so it's using your external storage

  • or maybe if the online compiler works for your board, however check licensing (for example if your code is still yours after compiling it there...)

Q: Importing an interface in a TypeScript file without generating a new directory structure A:

I think I've figured it out.

The solution I chanced upon was to rename ApiResponse.ts to ApiResponse.d.ts, remove the export, and put it into the include array in pub/tsconfig.json. This works well enough for this particular purpose; however, I'm not 100% on whether manually creating .d.ts files fits best practices.

Q: BackgroundService on Clean Architecture A:

Personally, I always put those kinds of services in the Presentation Layer in their minimal form, and I inject as much of the service logic as possible from the other layers, following the usual logic you probably follow everywhere else.
That said, the opposite is just as good.
There is no way in this world to have "zero" leaking between layers, as in the end you will always have a place where a layer connects to the other (as you said with Microsoft.Extension.Hosting.Abstractions).
I also don't consider the initial ASP.NET project a pure Presentation Layer, since it's also your composition root for dependency injection. Based on this logic (I don't want leaking), you would not be able to activate Entity Framework, considering EF is also activated with build.Services.
